claim: Nearly 1/3 of the human proteome is targeted to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) for folding and trafficking to downstream secretory pathway environments, including the extracellular space.
source: Nearly 1/3 of the human proteome is targeted to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) for folding and trafficking to downstream secretory pathway environments, including the extracellular space.
evidence: This is a statement about the proportion of the human proteome targeted to the ER, supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Secreted proteins engage ER-localized protein homeostasis factors such as chaperones and folding enzymes to facilitate their folding.
source: These secreted proteins engage ER-localized protein homeostasis (or proteostasis) factors such as chaperones and folding enzymes to facilitate their folding (Brodsky and Skach, 2011; Powers et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Brodsky and Skach, 2011; Powers et al., 2009).

claim: Proteins unable to fold in the ER are identified by ER proteostasis factors that direct them towards the proteasome (via ER-associated degradation) or lysosome for degradation.
source: Proteins unable to fold in the ER are identified by ER proteostasis factors that direct them towards the proteasome (via ER-associated degradation) or lysosome for degradation (Brodsky and Skach, 2011; Smith et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Brodsky and Skach, 2011; Smith et al., 2011).

claim: Partitioning toward degradation pathways prevents the folding and trafficking of destabilized, misfolding-prone proteins from the ER, which could aggregate into proteotoxic conformations in downstream secretory environments.
source: This partitioning toward degradation pathways prevents the folding and trafficking of destabilized, misfolding-prone proteins from the ER, which could aggregate into proteotoxic conformations in downstream secretory environments (Brodsky and Skach, 2011; Chen et al., 2011; Powers et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Brodsky and Skach, 2011; Chen et al., 2011; Powers et al., 2009).

claim: Many degenerative diseases result from imbalances in ER proteostasis.
source: Many degenerative diseases result from imbalances in ER proteostasis (Hipp et al., 2014; Luheshi et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Hipp et al., 2014; Luheshi et al., 2008).

claim: The aberrant secretion of properly folded, but destabilized aggregation-prone proteins facilitates extracellular proteotoxic aggregation associated with many amyloid diseases.
source: The aberrant secretion of properly folded, but destabilized aggregation-prone proteins facilitates extracellular proteotoxic aggregation associated with many amyloid diseases (Tipping et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Tipping et al., 2015).

claim: Transthyretin (TTR) amyloidosis and light chain (AL) amyloidosis are examples of diseases involving aberrant secretion of destabilized aggregation-prone proteins.
source: Examples include the transthyretin (TTR) or light chain (AL) amyloidoses (Blancas-Mejia and Ramirez-Alvarado, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Blancas-Mejia and Ramirez-Alvarado, 2013).

claim: The inability to efficiently degrade destabilized, aggregation-prone variants of rhodopsin facilitates proteotoxic intracellular aggregation linked to retinitis pigmentosa.
source: Similarly, the inability to efficiently degrade destabilized, aggregation-prone variants of secreted proteins such as rhodopsin and α-1-antitrypsin (A1AT) facilitates their proteotoxic intracellular aggregation linked to retinitis pigmentosa and liver disease, respectively (Gooptu et al., 2014; Lin and Lavail, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Gooptu et al., 2014; Lin and Lavail, 2010).

claim: The inability to efficiently degrade destabilized, aggregation-prone variants of α-1-antitrypsin (A1AT) facilitates proteotoxic intracellular aggregation linked to liver disease.
source: Similarly, the inability to efficiently degrade destabilized, aggregation-prone variants of secreted proteins such as rhodopsin and α-1-antitrypsin (A1AT) facilitates their proteotoxic intracellular aggregation linked to retinitis pigmentosa and liver disease, respectively (Gooptu et al., 2014; Lin and Lavail, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Gooptu et al., 2014; Lin and Lavail, 2010).

claim: Transcriptional reprogramming of the ER proteostasis network has the potential to increase the ER's capacity to identify destabilized, misfolding-prone proteins and prevent their secretion to downstream secretory environments.
source: One strategy to ameliorate the above-mentioned and related diseases is to transcriptionally reprogram the ER proteostasis network (ER PN), which has the potential to increase the ER's capacity to identify destabilized, misfolding-prone proteins and prevent their secretion to downstream secretory environments (Calamini and Morimoto, 2012; Chen et al., 2015; Gestwicki and Garza, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Calamini and Morimoto, 2012; Chen et al., 2015; Gestwicki and Garza, 2012).

claim: ER PN remodeling can be achieved by activation of the unfolded protein response (UPR), comprising three signaling pathways activated downstream of the ER stress sensing proteins IRE1, ATF6, and PERK.
source: ER PN remodeling can be achieved by activation of the unfolded protein response (UPR), comprising three signaling pathways activated downstream of the ER stress sensing proteins IRE1, ATF6, and PERK (Walter and Ron, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Walter and Ron, 2011).

claim: In response to the accumulation of misfolded proteins within the ER (i.e., ER stress), IRE1, ATF6, and PERK sensors are activated, resulting in ER PN reprogramming predominantly mediated by the UPR-associated transcription factors XBP1s and ATF6.
source: In response to the accumulation of misfolded proteins within the ER (i.e., ER stress), these sensors are activated, resulting in ER PN reprogramming predominantly mediated by the UPR-associated transcription factors XBP1s and ATF6.
evidence: This is a statement about the mechanism of UPR activation, supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: XBP1s and ATF6 transcription factors induce distinct, but overlapping, transcriptional programs that alter the composition of ER PN pathways.
source: These transcription factors induce distinct, but overlapping, transcriptional programs that alter the composition of ER PN pathways (Adachi et al., 2008; Shoulders et al., 2013; Yamamoto et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Adachi et al., 2008; Shoulders et al., 2013; Yamamoto et al., 2004).

claim: Genetic activation of the ATF6 transcriptional program attenuates intracellular accumulation of mutant rhodopsin.
source: Genetic activation of the ATF6 transcriptional program attenuates intracellular accumulation of mutant rhodopsin and the Z-variant of A1AT (Chiang et al., 2012; Smith et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Chiang et al., 2012; Smith et al., 2011).

claim: Genetic activation of the ATF6 transcriptional program attenuates intracellular accumulation of the Z-variant of A1AT.
source: Genetic activation of the ATF6 transcriptional program attenuates intracellular accumulation of mutant rhodopsin and the Z-variant of A1AT (Chiang et al., 2012; Smith et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Chiang et al., 2012; Smith et al., 2011).

claim: Stress-independent chemical genetic activation of a ligand-regulated ATF6 attenuates the secretion and extracellular aggregation of destabilized, amyloidogenic variants of TTR or immunoglobulin light chains (LCs), without significantly impacting secretion of stable, non-amyloidogenic variants of these proteins or the global endogenous secreted proteome.
source: Furthermore, stress-independent chemical genetic activation of a ligand-regulated ATF6 attenuates the secretion and extracellular aggregation of destabilized, amyloidogenic variants of TTR or immunoglobulin light chains (LCs), without significantly impacting secretion of stable, non-amyloidogenic variants of these proteins or the global endogenous secreted proteome (Chen et al., 2014; Cooley et al., 2014; Shoulders et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Chen et al., 2014; Cooley et al., 2014; Shoulders et al., 2013).

claim: Small molecules that induce preferential ER PN remodeling through pharmacologic activation of the ATF6 transcriptional program should attenuate the aberrant secretion and aggregation of proteins linked to degenerative diseases.
source: These results suggest that small molecules that similarly induce preferential ER PN remodeling through pharmacologic activation of the ATF6 transcriptional program should attenuate the aberrant secretion and aggregation of these proteins linked to degenerative diseases (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Chen et al., 2015) and represents a logical inference from previous results.

claim: Chronic addition of ER stressors such as thapsigargin or tunicamycin induces apoptosis, predominantly through activation of the PERK arm of the UPR.
source: However, chronic addition of these ER stressors induces apoptosis, predominantly through activation of the PERK arm of the UPR (Hetz, 2012; Tabas and Ron, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Hetz, 2012; Tabas and Ron, 2011).

claim: Small molecule kinase inhibitors and ATP mimetics have been shown to activate the IRE1/XBP1s arm of the UPR.
source: Small molecule kinase inhibitors and ATP mimetics have been shown to activate the IRE1/XBP1s arm of the UPR (Mendez et al., 2015; Papa et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Mendez et al., 2015; Papa et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2012).

claim: The small molecule BIX induces expression of the ATF6-target gene BiP through an ATF6-dependent mechanism.
source: The small molecule BIX induces expression of the ATF6-target gene BiP through an ATF6-dependent mechanism, but does not significantly induce expression of other ATF6 target genes such as GRP94, p58IPK and PDIA4, likely limiting its utility for ER PN reprogramming in the above-mentioned diseases (Kudo et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Kudo et al., 2008).

claim: BIX does not significantly induce expression of other ATF6 target genes such as GRP94, p58IPK and PDIA4.
source: The small molecule BIX induces expression of the ATF6-target gene BiP through an ATF6-dependent mechanism, but does not significantly induce expression of other ATF6 target genes such as GRP94, p58IPK and PDIA4, likely limiting its utility for ER PN reprogramming in the above-mentioned diseases (Kudo et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Kudo et al., 2008).

claim: An increasing proportion of failed clinical trials have highlighted the importance of the early elimination of compounds functioning through off-target effects, which can be achieved using multidimensional assays such as gene expression profiling.
source: An increasing proportion of failed clinical trials have highlighted the importance of the early elimination of compounds functioning through off-target effects, which can be achieved using multidimensional assays such as gene expression profiling (Feng et al., 2009; Verbist et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Feng et al., 2009; Verbist et al., 2015).

claim: The use of a transcriptional profiling approach early in the drug discovery process and before functional assessment allows for the identification of promising small molecules that preferentially activate a target transcriptional program, instead of global network activation.
source: The use of a transcriptional profiling approach early in the drug discovery process and before functional assessment allows for the identification of promising small molecules that preferentially activate a target transcriptional program, instead of global network activation.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of transcriptional profiling in drug discovery, supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Transcriptional profiling has only been employed in a small number of drug development programs and has not been used to identify small molecule activators of a sub-UPR transcriptional program, such as that regulated by ATF6.
source: However this strategy has only been employed in a small number of drug development programs and has not been used to identify small molecule activators of a sub-UPR transcriptional program, such as that regulated by ATF6 (Antipova et al., 2008; Stegmaier et al., 2004; Stegmaier et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Antipova et al., 2008; Stegmaier et al., 2004; Stegmaier et al., 2007).

claim: The authors employed a cell-based high-throughput screen (HTS) in combination with transcriptional profiling to identify non-toxic small molecules that preferentially activate the ATF6 transcriptional program, independent of global UPR activation.
source: Here, we employ a cell-based high-throughput screen (HTS) in combination with transcriptional profiling to identify non-toxic small molecules that preferentially activate the ATF6 transcriptional program, independent of global UPR activation.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's methodology and findings, supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Small molecule ER proteostasis regulators identified by the screening strategy mimic the ER PN reprogramming afforded by chemical genetic ATF6 activation, through a process dependent on endogenous ATF6.
source: Small molecule ER proteostasis regulators identified by our screening strategy mimic the ER PN reprogramming afforded by chemical genetic ATF6 activation, through a process dependent on endogenous ATF6.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings, supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The small molecule ER proteostasis regulators phenocopy the ability of chemical genetic ATF6 activation to preferentially decrease the secretion and proteotoxic aggregation of destabilized, amyloidogenic proteins without affecting the secretion of stable, non-amyloidogenic proteins or the global endogenous secreted proteome.
source: Furthermore, our small molecule ER proteostasis regulators phenocopy the ability of chemical genetic ATF6 activation to preferentially decrease the secretion and proteotoxic aggregation of destabilized, amyloidogenic proteins without affecting the secretion of stable, non-amyloidogenic proteins or the global endogenous secreted proteome.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings, supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The ERSE-FLuc reporter was preferentially activated by ATF6, relative to XBP1s in HEK293DAX cells.
source: As predicted, the ERSE-FLuc reporter was preferentially activated by ATF6, relative to XBP1s (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) in HEK293DAX cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The ERSE-FLuc reporter exhibited dose-dependent reporter activation upon treatment with the ER stressors Tg or Tm in HEK293T-Rex cells.
source: We then stably transfected the ERSE-FLuc reporter into HEK293T-Rex cells and selected a single clone exhibiting dose-dependent reporter activation upon treatment with the ER stressors Tg or Tm (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: The primary screen identified 13,799 molecules that activated the ERSE-FLuc reporter >25.1%.
source: This screen identified 13,799 molecules that activated the ERSE-FLuc reporter >25.1%.
evidence: This is a statement of the screening results, supported by the experimental data.

claim: Confirmation screening of 13,750 compounds identified 12,376 molecules that activated the ERSE-FLuc reporter 3 standard deviations above the DMSO control–a 90% hit confirmation.
source: Confirmation screening of the remaining 13,750 compounds identified 12,376 molecules that activated the ERSE-FLuc reporter 3 standard deviations above the DMSO control (hit cutoff 5.7% activation)–a 90% hit confirmation (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a statement of the screening results, supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Increasing the cutoff stringency to that used in the primary screen (25.1% activation) narrowed the list of ERSE-FLuc activators to 281 compounds.
source: To decrease the number of compounds for follow-up, we increased the cutoff stringency to that used in the primary screen (25.1% activation), which narrowed the list of ERSE-FLuc activators to 281 compounds (Figure 1E, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a statement of the screening results, supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The ER stressors Tg and Tm were both present in the SDDL and identified as hits.
source: These include the ER stressors Tg and Tm, which were both present in the SDDL.
evidence: This is a statement about the screening results, supported by the experimental data.

claim: A maximum common substructure search identified 12 chemical substructures that were highly represented in the 281 ERSE-FLuc activators.
source: A maximum common substructure search identified 12 chemical substructures that were highly represented in these 281 ERSE-FLuc activators (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is a statement of the analysis results, supported by the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: The highly represented chemical substructures in the 281 ERSE-FLuc activators include catechols (64/281), anilides (61/281) and benzylidene hydrazines (33/281).
source: These include catechols (64/281), anilides (61/281) and benzylidene hydrazines (33/281).
evidence: This is a statement of the analysis results, supported by the data.

claim: The XBP1-RLuc reporter contains Renilla luciferase (RLuc) expressed out of frame downstream of the XBP1 splice site, preventing RLuc translation in the absence of ER stress.
source: This reporter contains Renilla luciferase (RLuc) expressed out of frame downstream of the XBP1 splice site, preventing RLuc translation in the absence of ER stress (Figure 2A) (Back et al., 2006; Iwawaki et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a description of the reporter construct, supported by citations to published literature (Back et al., 2006; Iwawaki et al., 2004) and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In response to ER stress-dependent IRE1 activation, the 26-nt XBP1 intron is removed, producing a frame shift that allows for RLuc translation and luminescence.
source: In response to ER stress-dependent IRE1 activation, the 26-nt XBP1 intron is removed, producing a frame shift that allows for RLuc translation and luminescence.
evidence: This is a description of the mechanism of the reporter, supported by established knowledge of XBP1 splicing.

claim: Robust dose-dependent activation of the XBP1-RLuc reporter upon addition of the ER stressors Tg and Tm was confirmed in HEK293T-Rex cells stably expressing the XBP1-RLuc reporter, producing a Z' score of 0.75 for Tg.
source: Robust dose-dependent activation of the XBP1-RLuc reporter upon addition of the ER stressors Tg and Tm was confirmed in HEK293T-Rex cells stably expressing the XBP1-RLuc reporter, producing a Z' score of 0.75 for Tg (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is a statement of the experimental results, supported by the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Tg robustly activates both the ERSE-FLuc and XBP1-Rluc reporters, confirming the ability of this approach to identify global ER stressors.
source: Importantly, Tg (1 of the 281 screening hits) robustly activates both the ERSE-FLuc and XBP1-Rluc reporters, confirming the ability of this approach to identify global ER stressors (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a statement of the experimental results, supported by the data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The majority of molecules identified in the primary screen (200/281) activate the ERSE-FLuc reporter >2-fold better than the XBP1s-Rluc reporter.
source: In contrast, the majority of molecules identified in the primary screen (200/281) activate the ERSE-FLuc reporter >2-fold better than the XBP1s-Rluc reporter (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a statement of the experimental results, supported by the data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Small molecules identified from the HTS preferentially activate the ATF6 transcriptional program independent of ER stress and/or global UPR activation.
source: This suggests that small molecules identified from the HTS preferentially activate the ATF6 transcriptional program independent of ER stress and/or global UPR activation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results showing differential activation of the ERSE-FLuc and XBP1-RLuc reporters.

claim: Multiplex gene expression (MGE) profiling was performed in HEK293T-Rex cells treated with the 281 hits to directly monitor transcriptional changes and identify compounds that preferentially active the ATF6 transcriptional program.
source: As a final filter, we performed multiplex gene expression (MGE) profiling in HEK293T-Rex cells treated with the 281 hits to directly monitor transcriptional changes and identify compounds that preferentially active the ATF6 transcriptional program (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a statement of the methodology, supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Hierarchical clustering of the 281 screening hits based on the MGE data showed that compounds grouped into three distinct transcriptional profiles: 1) global UPR activators that activate ATF6, XBP1s and PERK target genes, 2) preferential activators of ATF6 targets, and 3) compounds with weak to no transcriptional effect.
source: We performed hierarchical clustering of the 281 screening hits based on the MGE data (Figure 2C). This showed that compounds grouped into three distinct transcriptional profiles: 1) global UPR activators that activate ATF6, XBP1s and PERK target genes (green), 2) preferential activators of ATF6 targets (pink), and 3) compounds with weak to no transcriptional effect.
evidence: This is a statement of the analysis results, supported by the data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Apart from the UPR, no compounds significantly induced gene targets regulated by other stress-responsive signaling pathways.
source: Apart from the UPR, no compounds significantly induced gene targets regulated by other stress-responsive signaling pathways (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a statement of the experimental results, supported by the data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Eighteen molecules, including the known ER stressors Tg and Tm, were identified to induce genes regulated by all three arms of the UPR, indicating that these molecules induce ER stress and/or global UPR activation.
source: Overall, eighteen molecules, including the known ER stressors Tg and Tm, were identified to induce genes regulated by all three arms of the UPR, indicating that these molecules induce ER stress and/or global UPR activation (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a statement of the experimental results, supported by the data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 79 compounds exhibited preferential activation of genes regulated in the ATF6 transcriptional program, relative to IRE1/XBP1s and PERK.
source: In contrast, 79 compounds exhibited preferential activation of genes regulated in the ATF6 transcriptional program, relative to IRE1/XBP1s and PERK.
evidence: This is a statement of the experimental results, supported by the data.

claim: 8 compounds were prioritized for further characterization based on their ability to preferentially activate the ATF6 transcriptional program with varying magnitude according to the MGE analysis.
source: We prioritized 8 compounds for further characterization (Table 1 — highlighted in Figure 2C). At this prioritization stage, we primarily focused on the MGE data and less emphasis was placed on the ATF6 or XBP1s luciferase reporter activation, as the MGE results provided richer information. The prioritized compounds were selected based on their ability to preferentially activate the ATF6 transcriptional program with varying magnitude according to the MGE analysis (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a statement of the selection criteria and results, supported by the data shown in Figure 2C and Table 1.

claim: The prioritized compounds demonstrated maximum toxicity of <10–43% that of doxorubicin, with all of them exhibiting a cytotoxic concentration 50% (CC50) of >17 μM.
source: The compounds demonstrated maximum toxicity of <10–43% that of doxorubicin, with all of them exhibiting a cytotoxic concentration 50% (CC50) of >17 μM (the highest tested concentration) (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a statement of the toxicity assessment results, supported by the data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: The three-tiered screening strategy allowed identification of generally non-toxic small molecule ER proteostasis regulators that preferentially activate the ATF6 transcriptional program.
source: These results suggest that our three-tiered screening strategy (Figure 1A) allowed identification of generally non-toxic small molecule ER proteostasis regulators that preferentially activate the ATF6 transcriptional program.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results, supported by the data shown in Figure 1A and the toxicity assessments.

claim: Compounds 132, 147, and 263 preferentially induce UPR-regulated genes involved in ER PN maintenance such as BiP, GRP94 and SEL1L.
source: This transcriptome analysis reveals that 132, 147, and 263 preferentially induce UPR-regulated genes involved in ER PN maintenance such as BiP, GRP94 and SEL1L (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C, red).
evidence: This is a statement of the mRNA-seq analysis results, supported by the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Compound 132 generated the most robust induction of UPR-regulated genes, relative to 147 and 263, consistent with the levels of ERSE-FLuc activation afforded by these molecules.
source: Compound 132 generated the most robust induction of these genes, relative to 147 and 263, consistent with the levels of ERSE-FLuc activation afforded by these molecules (Table 1).
evidence: This is a statement of the mRNA-seq analysis results, supported by the data.

claim: Compounds 132, 147, and 263 induced three genes that were not upregulated by Tg-dependent global UPR activation — HSPA1A, HSPA1B, and HMOX1.
source: Importantly, these small molecules induced three genes that were not upregulated by Tg-dependent global UPR activation — HSPA1A, HSPA1B, and HMOX1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: This is a statement of the mRNA-seq analysis results, supported by the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–F.

claim: HSPA1A and HSPA1B are transcriptional targets of the heat-shock response (HSR)-associated transcription factor HSF1.
source: HSPA1A and HSPA1B are transcriptional targets of the heat-shock response (HSR)-associated transcription factor HSF1 (Ryno et al., 2014) and HMOX1 is a transcriptional target of the oxidative stress response (Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Ryno et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2015).

claim: HMOX1 is a transcriptional target of the oxidative stress response.
source: HSPA1A and HSPA1B are transcriptional targets of the heat-shock response (HSR)-associated transcription factor HSF1 (Ryno et al., 2014) and HMOX1 is a transcriptional target of the oxidative stress response (Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Yang et al., 2015).

claim: Comparing the transcriptional profile previously observed for HSF1 activation to that observed for 132, 147, and 263 showed no significant correlation, indicating that these molecules do not induce the HSR.
source: Comparing the transcriptional profile previously observed for HSF1 activation (Ryno et al., 2014) to that observed for 132, 147, and 263 showed no significant correlation, indicating that these molecules do not induce the HSR (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G–J).
evidence: This is a statement of the analysis results, supported by the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G–J.

claim: The authors did not observe increased expression of oxidative stress markers, indicating that compounds 132, 147, and 263 do not globally activate the oxidative stress response.
source: Similarly, we did not observe increased expression of oxidative stress markers, indicating that these molecules do not globally activate the oxidative stress response (Figure 3—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: This is a statement of the analysis results, supported by the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1K.

claim: Compounds 132, 147, and 263 selectively induce UPR-regulated ER proteostasis genes independent of other stress-responsive signaling pathways.
source: These results confirm that our molecules selectively induce UPR-regulated ER proteostasis genes independent of other stress-responsive signaling pathways.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the mRNA-seq analysis results.

claim: Chemical genetic ATF6 activation in HEK293DAX cells selectively induces the ATF6 transcriptional program.
source: The ability of this approach to define preferential ER proteostasis remodeling was confirmed by demonstrating that chemical genetic ATF6 activation in HEK293DAX cells selectively induces the ATF6 transcriptional program (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is a statement of the experimental results, supported by the data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Compound 132 significantly activates the ATF6 transcriptional program (75% relative to Tg), but also robustly induces expression of IRE1/XBP1s and PERK genesets.
source: Compound 132 significantly activates the ATF6 transcriptional program (75% relative to Tg), but also robustly induces expression of IRE1/XBP1s and PERK genesets (Figure 3A,C).
evidence: This is a statement of the mRNA-seq analysis results, supported by the data shown in Figure 3A,C.

claim: Compound 132 is a global UPR activator.
source: While modest preferential activation of the ATF6 transcriptional program is observed, this indicates that 132 is a global UPR activator.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the mRNA-seq analysis results showing activation of multiple UPR arms.

claim: Compound 147 and to a lesser extent 263 show preferential activation of the ATF6 transcriptional program relative to IRE1/XBP1s and PERK, showing 45% and 50% activation relative to Tg, respectively.
source: In contrast, compound 147 and to a lesser extent 263 show preferential activation of the ATF6 transcriptional program relative to IRE1/XBP1s and PERK albeit to lower levels, showing 45% and 50% activation relative to Tg, respectively (Figure 3A,D,E).
evidence: This is a statement of the mRNA-seq analysis results, supported by the data shown in Figure 3A,D,E.

claim: Protein level changes induced by the addition of compounds 132, 147, or 263 correlated with transcript changes observed by mRNA-seq.
source: Protein level changes induced by the addition of these small molecules correlated with transcript changes observed by mRNA-seq (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is a statement of the proteomics analysis results, supported by the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: Compound 132 increased levels of proteins regulated downstream of ATF6, IRE1/XBP1s and PERK to similar extents, further confirming that 132 is a global UPR activator.
source: Applying an analogous geneset analysis to that described above showed that 132 increased levels of proteins regulated downstream of ATF6, IRE1/XBP1s and PERK to similar extents, further confirming that 132 is a global UPR activator (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a statement of the proteomics analysis results, supported by the data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Compounds 147 and 263 preferentially increased levels of proteins regulated by the ATF6 transcriptional program, further confirming that these molecules reprogram the ER PN through a mechanism involving preferential activation of this transcriptional program.
source: However, 147 and 263 preferentially increased levels of proteins regulated by the ATF6 transcriptional program, further confirming that these molecules reprogram the ER PN through a mechanism involving preferential activation of this transcriptional program (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: This is a statement of the proteomics analysis results, supported by the data shown in Figure 3G,H.

claim: Neither compound 147 nor 263 showed significant increases in ERSE-FLuc activation at concentrations >10 µM.
source: When monitoring the activation of the ATF6-selective ERSE-FLuc reporter in HEK293 cells treated with increasing concentrations of 147 and 263 (Figure 3I,J), neither compound showed significant increases in ERSE-FLuc activation at concentrations >10 µM – the concentration used for mRNA-seq.
evidence: This is a statement of the experimental results, supported by the data shown in Figure 3I,J.

claim: Increasing the concentration of compounds 147 and 263 did not significantly increase activation of the IRE1/XBP1s-selective XBP1-RLuc reporter.
source: Similarly, increasing the concentration of these molecules did not significantly increase activation of the IRE1/XBP1s-selective XBP1-RLuc reporter.
evidence: This is a statement of the experimental results.

claim: A maximal BiP induction at 6 hr in cells treated with 147 or 263 over a 24 hr time course was observed, with no time-dependent increases in expression of the XBP1s target Sec24D.
source: Furthermore, we observe a maximal BiP induction at 6 hr in cells treated with 147 or 263 over a 24 hr time course and no time-dependent increases in expression of the XBP1s target Sec24D (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E–F).
evidence: This is a statement of the experimental results, supported by the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E–F.

claim: Increasing the concentration or duration of treatment with small molecule ER proteostasis regulators does not alter their preferential activation of the ATF6 transcriptional program, suggesting that the compounds do not function by inducing a mild level of ER stress.
source: These results indicate that increasing the concentration or duration of treatment with small molecule ER proteostasis regulators does not alter their preferential activation of the ATF6 transcriptional program, suggesting that the compounds do not function by inducing a mild level of ER stress.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results showing no dose- or time-dependent increases in XBP1s activation.

claim: All 8 prioritized small molecule ER proteostasis regulators induced BiP expression in ATF6+/+ MEF cells, albeit to varying extents.
source: Expression of the ATF6 target gene BiP was measured in ATF6+/+ mouse embryonic fibroblast (MEF) cells treated with the top 8 prioritized small molecule ER proteostasis regulators shown in Table 1. All of these molecules induced BiP expression in these cells, albeit to varying extents (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a statement of the experimental results, supported by the data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: BiP induction was significantly inhibited in the ATF6-/- MEFs, showing that small molecule-dependent upregulation of a gene included in the ATF6 transcriptional program requires endogenous ATF6.
source: In contrast, BiP induction was significantly inhibited in the ATF6-/- MEFs, showing that small molecule-dependent upregulation of a gene included in the ATF6 transcriptional program requires endogenous ATF6.
evidence: This is a statement of the experimental results showing dependence on ATF6.

claim: The authors did not observe significant levels of XBP1 splicing or eIF2α phosphorylation in cells treated with the ER proteostasis regulators, indicating that these molecules do not significantly activate the IRE1/XBP1s or PERK arms of the UPR.
source: Importantly, we did not observe significant levels of XBP1 splicing or eIF2α phosphorylation in cells treated with the ER proteostasis regulators, indicating that these molecules do not significantly activate the IRE1/XBP1s or PERK arms of the UPR (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is a statement of the experimental results, supported by the data shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: Treatment with small molecules 132 and 263 increased the nuclear fraction of ATF6-GFP, reflecting increased ATF6 processing.
source: Treatment with small molecules 132 and 263 increased the nuclear fraction of ATF6-GFP, reflecting increased ATF6 processing (Figure 4D—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a statement of the experimental results, supported by the data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Compound 132 and 263 treatment led to increased accumulation of the 50 kDa ATF6 fragment, resulting from S1P/S2P endoproteolysis in the Golgi, as shown by immunoblotting.
source: Compound 132 and 263 treatment also led to increased accumulation of the 50 kDa ATF6 fragment, resulting from S1P/S2P endoproteolysis in the Golgi, as shown by immunoblotting (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a statement of the experimental results, supported by the data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Other molecules, including 147, did not significantly increase ATF6-GFP nuclear localization or accumulation of the 50 kDa ATF6 fragment, although it cannot be excluded that they also induce ATF6 processing, albeit to a lower extent that falls outside the dynamic range or sensitivity of these assays.
source: Other molecules, including 147, did not significantly increase ATF6-GFP nuclear localization or accumulation of the 50 kDa ATF6 fragment, although it cannot be excluded that they also induce ATF6 processing, albeit to a lower extent that falls outside the dynamic range or sensitivity of these assays.
evidence: This is a statement of the experimental results with a caveat about assay sensitivity.

claim: PF-429242 inhibited the activation of ERSE-FLuc in cells treated with all 8 ER proteostasis regulators, reflecting the dependence of the small molecules on S1P proteolysis for ATF6 activation.
source: PF-429242 also inhibited the activation of ERSE-FLuc in cells treated with all 8 ER proteostasis regulators (Figure 4E), reflecting the dependence of our small molecules on S1P proteolysis for ATF6 activation.
evidence: This is a statement of the experimental results, supported by the data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The small molecule ER proteostasis regulators activate the ATF6 transcriptional program through a mechanism involving S1P-dependent processing of endogenous ATF6.
source: Collectively, the ATF6 knockout, nuclear localization and S1P inhibition results indicate that the small molecule ER proteostasis regulators activate the ATF6 transcriptional program through a mechanism involving S1P-dependent processing of endogenous ATF6.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results from ATF6 knockout, nuclear localization, and S1P inhibition experiments.

claim: Compounds 147 and 263 induced expression of the ATF6-target gene BiP in HepG2 cells by qPCR.
source: We confirmed that 147 and 263 induced expression of the ATF6-target gene BiP in HepG2 cells by qPCR (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a statement of the experimental results, supported by the data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Treatment with 10 µM of compounds 147 and 263 does not influence HepG2 viability, although higher concentrations (100 µM) do reduce viability.
source: We also showed that the treatment dose of these small molecules (10 µM) does not influence HepG2 viability, although higher concentrations (100 µM) do reduce viability (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a statement of the experimental results, supported by the data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Pretreatment with Tg reduced secretion of both FTTTRA25T and FTTTRWT.
source: Pretreatment with Tg reduced secretion of both FTTTRA25T and FTTTRWT (Figure 5B—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a statement of the experimental results, supported by the data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Pretreatment with 147 and 263 reduced FTTTRA25T secretion by 45%, but did not significantly influence secretion of FTTTRWT.
source: However, pretreatment with 147 and 263 reduced FTTTRA25T secretion by 45%, but did not significantly influence secretion of FTTTRWT (Figure 5B—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a statement of the experimental results, supported by the data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The reduction in FTTTRA25T secretion induced by compounds 147 and 263 correlates with increased degradation of FTTTRA25T.
source: The reduction in FTTTRA25T secretion induced by these molecules correlates with increased degradation of FTTTRA25T (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a statement of the experimental results, supported by the data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The selective reduction in secretion and increase in degradation for FTTTRA25T induced by 147 and 263 is strictly analogous to that observed after chemical genetic ATF6 activation in HepG2ATF6 cells.
source: Notably, the selective reduction in secretion and increase in degradation for FTTTRA25T induced by 147 and 263 is strictly analogous to that observed after chemical genetic ATF6 activation in these cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,E) (Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement comparing the experimental results to previously published data, supported by the data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,E and a citation (Chen et al., 2014).

claim: Small molecule ER proteostasis regulators 147 and 263 phenocopy the capacity of chemical genetic ATF6 activation to selectively reduce secretion of destabilized, amyloidogenic TTR variants relative to the wild-type protein.
source: This indicates that these small molecule ER proteostasis regulators phenocopy the capacity of chemical genetic ATF6 activation to selectively reduce secretion of destabilized, amyloidogenic TTR variants relative to the wild-type protein.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results showing selective reduction of FTTTRA25T secretion.

claim: Treatment with the ER stressor Tg significantly reduced the recovery of [35S] labeled proteins in conditioned media, consistent with the ability of ER stress to induce translational attenuation and globally disrupt protein secretion.
source: Treatment with the ER stressor Tg significantly reduced the recovery of [35S] labeled proteins in conditioned media, consistent with the ability of ER stress to induce translational attenuation and globally disrupt protein secretion (Figure 5D—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is a statement of the experimental results, supported by the data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Chemical genetic ATF6 activation, or pharmacologic activation of the ATF6 transcriptional program through addition of compound 147 or 263, did not influence the levels of [35S] labeled proteins in media, demonstrating that preferential ATF6 activation does not globally disrupt secretion of the endogenous proteome.
source: However, chemical genetic ATF6 activation, or pharmacologic activation of the ATF6 transcriptional program through addition of compound 147 or 263, did not influence the levels of [35S] labeled proteins in media, demonstrating that preferential ATF6 activation does not globally disrupt secretion of the endogenous proteome.
evidence: This is a statement of the experimental results showing no effect on global protein secretion.

claim: Chemical genetic ATF6 activation reduces secretion and extracellular aggregation of ALLC without notably affecting secretion of a stable, non-amyloidogenic LC.
source: Chemical genetic ATF6 activation reduces secretion and extracellular aggregation of ALLC without notably affecting secretion of a stable, non-amyloidogenic LC (Cooley et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Cooley et al., 2014).

claim: Compound 147 induced expression of the ATF6 target gene BiP in ALMC-2 cells but 263 did not.
source: Compound 147 induced expression of the ATF6 target gene BiP in ALMC-2 cells but unexpectedly, 263 did not (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a statement of the experimental results, supported by the data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Treatment with compound 147 reduced ALLC secretion >50% from ALMC-2 cells, as measured by an ELISA while 263 did not significantly influence ALLC secretion.
source: Treatment with compound 147 reduced ALLC secretion >50% from ALMC-2 cells, as measured by an ELISA while 263 did not significantly influence ALLC secretion (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a statement of the experimental results, supported by the data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Dose-dependent treatment with 147 measuring ALLC secretion afforded an EC50 value of 1.1 µM.
source: Dose-dependent treatment with 147 measuring ALLC secretion afforded an EC50 value of 1.1 µM (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a statement of the experimental results, supported by the data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The attenuation in ALLC secretion saturated above 10 µM, producing a similar dose-response curve to 147-dependent ATF6 reporter activation.
source: The attenuation in ALLC secretion saturated above 10 µM, producing a similar dose-response curve to 147-dependent ATF6 reporter activation (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is a statement of the experimental results, supported by the data shown in Figure 3I and Figure 6C.

claim: Compounds 147 and 263 only minimally affected the secretion of an energetically normal, fully assembled IgG from a control KAS-6/1 plasma cell line isolated from a multiple myeloma patient that did not present with AL.
source: Conversely, compared to the reduction in ALLC secretion, these molecules only minimally affected the secretion of an energetically normal, fully assembled IgG from a control KAS-6/1 plasma cell line isolated from a multiple myeloma patient that did not present with AL (Figure 6D) (Westendorf et al., 1996).
evidence: This is a statement of the experimental results, supported by the data shown in Figure 6D and a citation (Westendorf et al., 1996).

claim: Small molecule ER proteostasis regulators that preferentially activate the ATF6 transcriptional program, e.g., 147, selectively reduce secretion of destabilized, amyloidogenic LCs, but not IgGs.
source: These data indicate that small molecule ER proteostasis regulators that preferentially activate the ATF6 transcriptional program, e.g., 147, selectively reduce secretion of destabilized, amyloidogenic LCs, but not IgGs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results showing selective reduction of ALLC secretion but not IgG secretion.

claim: Tg treatment reduced viability of ALMC-2 and KAS-6/1 cells.
source: Tg treatment reduced viability of ALMC-2 and KAS-6/1 cells (Figure 6B,D).
evidence: This is a statement of the experimental results, supported by the data shown in Figure 6B,D.

claim: The preferential activator of the ATF6 transcriptional program, 147, only minimally influenced the viability of ALMC-2 or KAS-6/1 cells, suggesting that the reductions in ALLC secretion afforded by this molecule involve reprogramming of the ER PN.
source: However, the preferential activator of the ATF6 transcriptional program, 147, only minimally influenced the viability of ALMC-2 or KAS-6/1 cells (Figure 6B–D), suggesting that the reductions in ALLC secretion afforded by this molecule involve reprogramming of the ER PN.
evidence: This is a statement of the experimental results and an inference about the mechanism, supported by the data shown in Figure 6B–D.

claim: Small molecule-dependent reductions in ALLC secretion from ALMC-2 cells strongly correlate with BiP induction in these cells.
source: Consistent with this prediction, small molecule-dependent reductions in ALLC secretion from ALMC-2 cells strongly correlate with BiP induction in these cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a statement of the analysis results, supported by the data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Immunopurification of ALLC from ALMC-2 cells pretreated with 147 and subjected to in situ crosslinking showed increased interactions between ALLC and the ATF6-regulated chaperones BiP and GRP94.
source: Furthermore, immunopurification of ALLC from ALMC-2 cells pretreated with 147 and subjected to in situ crosslinking showed increased interactions between ALLC and the ATF6-regulated chaperones BiP and GRP94 (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a statement of the experimental results, supported by the data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Pretreatment with 263, which did not induce BiP in ALMC-2 cells, did not increase the co-isolation of BiP and GRP94 chaperones with ALLC.
source: However, pretreatment with 263, which did not induce BiP in ALMC-2 cells, did not increase the co-isolation of these chaperones.
evidence: This is a statement of the experimental results.

claim: Pharmacologic reductions in ALLC secretion are linked to reprogramming of the ER proteostasis environment.
source: These results suggest that pharmacologic reductions in ALLC secretion are linked to reprogramming of the ER proteostasis environment.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results showing correlation between BiP induction and ALLC secretion reduction, and increased chaperone interactions.

claim: Chemical genetic ATF6 activation reduces ALLC secretion through a mechanism involving prolonged ER retention.
source: We previously showed that chemical genetic ATF6 activation reduces ALLC secretion through a mechanism involving prolonged ER retention (Cooley et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Cooley et al., 2014).

claim: Genetic XBP1s activation reduces ALLC secretion by increasing its degradation.
source: In contrast, genetic XBP1s activation reduces ALLC secretion by increasing its degradation.
evidence: This is a statement about the mechanism of XBP1s activation, supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: A cycloheximide chase assay demonstrated that pretreatment with 147 reduced ALLC secretion by 30% through a mechanism involving increased ER retention.
source: A cycloheximide chase assay demonstrated that pretreatment with 147 reduced ALLC secretion by 30% through a mechanism involving increased ER retention (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E–G).
evidence: This is a statement of the experimental results, supported by the data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E–G.

claim: Compound 147 reduces secretion of ALLC through a mechanism similar or identical to that previously observed with chemical genetic ATF6 activation.
source: This indicates that 147 reduces secretion of ALLC through a mechanism similar or identical to that previously observed with chemical genetic ATF6 activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results showing increased ER retention.

claim: Treatment with 147 decreased extracellular ALLC aggregates by >50%.
source: Treatment with 147 decreased extracellular ALLC aggregates by >50% (Figure 6F—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is a statement of the experimental results, supported by the data shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Similar reduction in aggregation was observed for additional ER proteostasis regulators tested that lowered ALLC secretion.
source: Similar reduction in aggregation was observed for additional ER proteostasis regulators tested that lowered ALLC secretion (Figure 6F—figure supplement 1H,I).
evidence: This is a statement of the experimental results, supported by the data shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1H,I.

claim: The reduction in ALLC secretion afforded by the ER proteostasis regulators attenuates extracellular LC aggregation.
source: This indicates that the reduction in ALLC secretion afforded by our ER proteostasis regulators attenuates extracellular LC aggregation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results showing reduced ALLC aggregation.

claim: Reprogramming of subcellular proteostasis environments through activation of stress-responsive signaling pathways is a promising strategy to restore mutant protein folding or enhance mutant protein degradation.
source: Reprogramming of subcellular proteostasis environments through activation of stress-responsive signaling pathways is a promising strategy to restore mutant protein folding or enhance mutant protein degradation (Calamini and Morimoto, 2012; Chen et al., 2015; Das et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Calamini and Morimoto, 2012; Chen et al., 2015; Das et al., 2015).

claim: Pharmacologic activation of the ATF6 transcriptional program requires S1P-dependent processing of endogenous ATF6.
source: We show that pharmacologic activation of the ATF6 transcriptional program requires S1P-dependent processing of endogenous ATF6.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results from S1P inhibition experiments.

claim: The small molecule ER proteostasis regulators phenocopy the capacity of chemical genetic ATF6 activation to selectively reduce secretion and extracellular aggregation of destabilized amyloidogenic variants of proteins such as TTR and LC.
source: Furthermore, we show that our small molecule ER proteostasis regulators phenocopy the capacity of chemical genetic ATF6 activation to selectively reduce secretion and extracellular aggregation of destabilized amyloidogenic variants of proteins such as TTR and LC.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings, supported by the experimental data.

claim: The phenotypic screening approach sought to identify small molecule ER proteostasis regulators that activated the ATF6 transcriptional program, without placing a constraint for the compounds to act directly on ATF6.
source: Our phenotypic screening approach sought to identify small molecule ER proteostasis regulators that activated the ATF6 transcriptional program, without placing a constraint for the compounds to act directly on ATF6.
evidence: This is a statement about the screening strategy.

claim: Prioritized compounds such as 147 and 263 function through a mechanism that requires endogenous ATF6.
source: Nonetheless, prioritized compounds such as 147 and 263 function through a mechanism that requires endogenous ATF6.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results from ATF6 knockout experiments.

claim: ATF6 is activated through a mechanism distinct to that utilized by the two other arms of the UPR.
source: ATF6 is activated through a mechanism distinct to that utilized by the two other arms of the UPR.
evidence: This is a statement about the mechanism of ATF6 activation, supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: In response to ER stress, ATF6 traffics to the Golgi where it is endoproteolytically processed by S1P and S2P.
source: In response to ER stress, ATF6 traffics to the Golgi where it is endoproteolytically processed by S1P and S2P (Ye et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Ye et al., 2000).

claim: S1P and S2P processing releases the ATF6 bZIP transcription factor into the cytosol, facilitating its translocation to the nucleus where it promotes induction of the ATF6 transcriptional program.
source: This releases the ATF6 bZIP transcription factor into the cytosol, facilitating its translocation to the nucleus where it promotes induction of the ATF6 transcriptional program.
evidence: This is a statement about the mechanism of ATF6 activation, supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: ATF6 is not known to contain any allosteric small molecule binding sites.
source: ATF6 is not known to contain any allosteric small molecule binding sites.
evidence: This is a statement about the current knowledge of ATF6 structure.

claim: It is likely that the small molecules promote ATF6 activation through interactions with proteins that regulate its activity such as BiP and the PDIs.
source: Thus, it is likely that our molecules promote ATF6 activation through interactions with proteins that regulate its activity such as BiP and the PDIs.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism of action of the small molecules.

claim: BiP and PDIs are predicted to be involved in initiating ATF6 trafficking to the Golgi, although their role in this process remains poorly defined.
source: Both of these are predicted to be involved in initiating ATF6 trafficking to the Golgi, although their role in this process remains poorly defined (Nadanaka et al., 2007; Shen et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Nadanaka et al., 2007; Shen et al., 2002).

claim: The small molecules could also preferentially induce ATF6 activity by targeting or mimicking metabolites required for activation of this pathway.
source: Our small molecules could also preferentially induce ATF6 activity by targeting or mimicking metabolites required for activation of this pathway.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism of action of the small molecules.

claim: Previous work shows that PERK and IRE1 can be activated independent of ATF6 in response to alterations in cellular lipid composition.
source: Previous work shows that PERK and IRE1 can be activated independent of ATF6 in response to alterations in cellular lipid composition (Volmer et al., 2013) but no such mechanism has been reported for ATF6 to date.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Volmer et al., 2013).

claim: ER proteostasis regulators identified in the screen appear to preferentially induce ATF6 activation through distinct mechanisms.
source: Interestingly, ER proteostasis regulators identified in our screen appear to preferentially induce ATF6 activation through distinct mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of cell type-specific effects.

claim: Compound 263 demonstrates varying levels of BiP induction in distinct cell types (e.g., 263 induces BiP in HEK293T and HepG2 cells, but not in ALMC-2 cells).
source: This is evident for molecules such as 263, which demonstrates varying levels of BiP induction in distinct cell types (e.g., 263 induces BiP in HEK293T and HepG2 cells, but not in ALMC-2 cells).
evidence: This is a statement of the experimental results showing cell type-specific effects.

claim: Compound 147 activates the ATF6 pathway in all cell types tested.
source: This is in contrast to compound 147 that activates the ATF6 pathway in all cell types tested.
evidence: This is a statement of the experimental results.

claim: The capacity to activate ATF6 in a cell type specific fashion could be harnessed to define the underlying molecular mechanisms involved in ATF6 activation and develop compounds that induce tissue-selective ER PN remodeling.
source: This capacity to activate ATF6 in a cell type specific fashion could be harnessed to define the underlying molecular mechanisms involved in ATF6 activation and develop compounds that induce tissue-selective ER PN remodeling.
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential utility of the cell type-specific effects.

claim: One mechanism by which the ATF6 transcriptional program influences ER function is by increasing the stringency of ER protein quality control.
source: One mechanism by which the ATF6 transcriptional program influences ER function is by increasing the stringency of ER protein quality control (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Chen et al., 2015).

claim: Stress-independent ATF6 activation selectively attenuates the secretion and subsequent proteotoxic aggregation of destabilized, disease-associated proteins without affecting the secretion of the endogenous proteome.
source: Stress-independent ATF6 activation selectively attenuates the secretion and subsequent proteotoxic aggregation of destabilized, disease-associated proteins without affecting the secretion of the endogenous proteome (Chen et al., 2014; Chiang et al., 2012; Cooley et al., 2014; Shoulders et al., 2013; Smith et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Chen et al., 2014; Chiang et al., 2012; Cooley et al., 2014; Shoulders et al., 2013; Smith et al., 2011).

claim: The top small molecule ER proteostasis regulators (e.g., 147) phenocopy the ability of chemical genetic ATF6 activation to selectively reduce secretion of destabilized, disease-associated variants of amyloidogenic proteins such as TTR and immunoglobulin LC.
source: Our top small molecule ER proteostasis regulators (e.g., 147) phenocopy the ability of chemical genetic ATF6 activation to selectively reduce secretion of destabilized, disease-associated variants of amyloidogenic proteins such as TTR and immunoglobulin LC.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings, supported by the experimental data.

claim: The small molecules could similarly phenocopy the ATF6-dependent reductions in the trafficking and intracellular aggregation of destabilized, aggregation-prone proteins associated with other gain-of-toxicity protein misfolding diseases (e.g., A1AT-Z aggregation in liver disease and rhodopsin aggregation in retinal degeneration).
source: This suggests that our small molecules could similarly phenocopy the ATF6-dependent reductions in the trafficking and intracellular aggregation of destabilized, aggregation-prone proteins associated with other gain-of-toxicity protein misfolding diseases (e.g., A1AT-Z aggregation in liver disease and rhodopsin aggregation in retinal degeneration (Chiang et al., 2012; Smith et al., 2011)).
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential utility of the small molecules, supported by citations to published literature (Chiang et al., 2012; Smith et al., 2011).

claim: Small molecule ER proteostasis regulators identified have the potential to broadly ameliorate degenerative diseases associated with aggregation of secretory proteins.
source: Thus, small molecule ER proteostasis regulators identified herein have the potential to broadly ameliorate degenerative diseases associated with aggregation of secretory proteins.
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential therapeutic utility of the small molecules.

claim: The long-term consequences of periodic pharmacologic activation of the ATF6 arm of the UPR are unclear.
source: The long-term consequences of periodic pharmacologic activation of the ATF6 arm of the UPR are unclear.
evidence: This is a statement acknowledging uncertainty about long-term effects.

claim: Mechanism-based toxicity associated with adapting ER proteostasis to ameliorate secretory protein misfolding and/or aggregation is possible.
source: Mechanism-based toxicity associated with adapting ER proteostasis to ameliorate secretory protein misfolding and/or aggregation is possible.
evidence: This is a statement acknowledging potential toxicity concerns.

claim: A subset of compounds, especially compounds that preferentially activate the ATF6 transcriptional program (e.g., 147), show no significant toxicity across multiple cell models.
source: While some small molecule ER proteostasis regulators identified show mild toxicity, a subset of compounds, especially compounds that preferentially activate the ATF6 transcriptional program (e.g., 147), show no significant toxicity across multiple cell models.
evidence: This is a statement of the toxicity assessment results.

claim: The lack of significant toxicity of compounds like 147 likely reflects the limited activation of the IRE1/XBP1s and PERK arms of the UPR afforded by these molecules, minimizing apoptosis signaling induced downstream of these two UPR signaling pathways.
source: This likely reflects the limited activation of the IRE1/XBP1s and PERK arms of the UPR afforded by these molecules, minimizing apoptosis signaling induced downstream of these two UPR signaling pathways (Hetz, 2012; Tabas and Ron, 2011).
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism of low toxicity, supported by citations to published literature (Hetz, 2012; Tabas and Ron, 2011).

claim: The moderate levels of ATF6 activation achieved using the small molecule ER proteostasis regulators likely also minimize pathologic imbalances in ER function.
source: The moderate levels of ATF6 activation achieved using our small molecule ER proteostasis regulators likely also minimize pathologic imbalances in ER function.
evidence: This is a speculation about the safety of moderate ATF6 activation.

claim: High levels of ATF6 activation induce hepatic steatosis in zebrafish, whereas lower levels do not.
source: It is known that high levels of ATF6 activation induce hepatic steatosis in zebrafish, whereas lower levels do not (Howarth et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Howarth et al., 2014).

claim: The low molecular weight and structural simplicity of the small molecules identified by the multi-tiered screening strategy (e.g., 147) provides a significant amount of chemical space that can be explored through structure-activity relationships to optimize potency, selectivity and dosing regimens, while minimizing toxicity.
source: Finally, the low molecular weight and structural simplicity of the small molecules identified by our multi-tiered screening strategy (e.g., 147) provides a significant amount of chemical space that can be explored through structure-activity relationships to optimize potency, selectivity and dosing regimens, while minimizing toxicity.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential for medicinal chemistry optimization.

claim: Several of the prioritized molecules include functional groups found in pan-assay interference compounds (PAINS), but given that these ER proteostasis regulators showed activity in multiple complementary screening assays, they are unlikely to act through off-target pathways.
source: Several of our prioritized molecules include functional groups found in pan-assay interference compounds (PAINS) (Baell and Walters, 2014), but given that these ER proteostasis regulators showed activity in multiple complementary screening assays, they are unlikely to act through off-target pathways.
evidence: This is a statement addressing potential concerns about PAINS, supported by the multi-assay validation and a citation (Baell and Walters, 2014).

claim: The molecules depend on ATF6 and its canonical activation pathway for the induction of ATF6 target genes.
source: Consistent with this, the molecules depend on ATF6 and its canonical activation pathway for the induction of ATF6 target genes.
evidence: This is a statement of the experimental results showing ATF6 dependence.

claim: The RNA-Seq and proteomics profiling analysis for 147 and 263 confirmed that these molecules exert very little off-target transcriptome changes and proteome remodeling apart from preferential ER PN activation.
source: Furthermore, the RNA-Seq and proteomics profiling analysis for 147 and 263 confirmed that these molecules exert very little off-target transcriptome changes and proteome remodeling apart from preferential ER PN activation.
evidence: This is a statement of the analysis results showing specificity.

claim: Both 147 and 263 contain functional groups that after metabolic oxidation to a quinone methide could modify proteins covalently.
source: Both 147 and 263 contain functional groups that after metabolic oxidation to a quinone methide could modify proteins covalently.
evidence: This is a statement about the chemical properties of the molecules.

claim: The covalent modification of ATF6 or a protein involved in the regulation of ATF6 activity (e.g., BiP or PDIs) by the small molecules could be involved in the activation mechanism.
source: This suggests that the covalent modification of ATF6 or a protein involved in the regulation of ATF6 activity (e.g., BiP or PDIs) (Nadanaka et al., 2007; Shen et al., 2002) by our small molecules could be involved in the activation mechanism.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism of action, supported by citations to published literature (Nadanaka et al., 2007; Shen et al., 2002).

claim: Future medicinal chemistry efforts will focus on exploring the mechanism of action of these compounds and the potential involvement of covalent protein modification for their activity.
source: Future medicinal chemistry efforts will focus on exploring the mechanism of action of these compounds and the potential involvement of covalent protein modification for their activity.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: The establishment of ER proteostasis regulators, such as 147, provides a unique opportunity to define the underlying molecular mechanism(s) of ATF6 activation and to probe the involvement of ATF6 in regulating ER PN function.
source: The establishment of ER proteostasis regulators, such as 147, provides a unique opportunity to define the underlying molecular mechanism(s) of ATF6 activation and to probe the involvement of ATF6 in regulating ER PN function.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential utility of the small molecules for research.

claim: These molecules represent a valuable resource to define the therapeutic potential of ATF6 transcriptional program activation to correct pathologic imbalances in ER proteostasis in cellular and animal models of protein misfolding and aggregation diseases.
source: These molecules also represent a valuable resource to define the therapeutic potential of ATF6 transcriptional program activation to correct pathologic imbalances in ER proteostasis in cellular and animal models of protein misfolding and aggregation diseases.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential utility of the small molecules for therapeutic development.

claim: As the authors continue to develop the top small molecule ER proteostasis regulators through medicinal chemistry, they will establish second generation molecules that optimize ER PN reprogramming to ameliorate pathologic imbalances in ER proteostasis associated with diverse protein aggregation diseases such as the systemic amyloidosis.
source: As we continue to develop our top small molecule ER proteostasis regulators through medicinal chemistry, we will establish second generation molecules that optimize ER PN reprogramming to ameliorate pathologic imbalances in ER proteostasis associated with diverse protein aggregation diseases such as the systemic amyloidosis.
evidence: This is a statement about future research and development plans.
